title: Confirm a suspected duct stone before invasive treatment
fairness: MRCP is the single best offered investigation: persistent cholestatic abnormalities and duct enlargement warrant duct assessment, but neither a demonstrated stone nor an infected obstruction is supplied. EUS is not offered, and the explanation appropriately acknowledges it.

The resident must localize the unresolved problem to the duct and distinguish confirmation from therapeutic ERCP. Normal bilirubin and settled pain do not automatically settle the duct question. HIDA represents a different, credible biliary-workup error.

The negative inflammatory observations are relevant to the competing HIDA path rather than a nonmedical answer shortcut. The full investigation names have comparable grammar and specificity. The standalone task is complete.

Review scope for this report: all 18 current proposals, comprising seven rewrites and eleven new items, including the eleven pass-preserved proposals, were independently assessed from their after fields. Six kept inventory records, 42 historical retirement/replacement proposals, 16 parked attempts and the recorded held/unkeyed material were noted but not scored. Archived v1 candidates and author verdicts did not determine these judgments.

All difficulty and high-yield judgments are qualitative editorial estimates. This is an offline content review, not fresh guideline/source verification, runtime wait/randomization validation or clinical approval. Every draft still requires Melissa Rowland's exact-version clinical sign-off. These limitations apply to every entry.

title: Reassess duct-stone suspicion after a negative MRCP
fairness: EUS is the best offered test for renewed suspicion after a negative interval MRCP. Recurrence and new cholestatic abnormalities make the prior negative result insufficient to close the question, while the current comfortable, afebrile state and lack of a demonstrated stone do not establish a therapeutic ERCP indication.

Two consequential judgments remain: reassess the meaning of the earlier negative study in light of the later episode, then choose a confirmatory rather than invasive therapeutic pathway. The task identifies a duct question but does not supply either judgment.

HIDA is the weaker competitor because the task is already duct-focused; ERCP remains a credible close error. There is no key-only wording overlap or length outlier. The standalone chronology is coherent, and the explanation does not claim that every negative MRCP requires EUS.

title: Choose gallbladder filling rather than emptying assessment
fairness: Gallbladder-filling scintigraphy is the best offered protocol for persistent focal and systemic inflammatory findings despite an adequately visualized ultrasound lacking wall thickening or surrounding fluid.

The resident must interpret the clinical-ultrasound discrepancy and then distinguish an acute filling question from stimulated emptying or duct mapping. The two scintigraphic choices prevent generic recall of HIDA from uniquely answering the question.

The observations do not name acute cholecystitis or teach the filling rule before the choice. All options are examination protocols of comparable specificity. The recorded admission stage is clear, and this active case stands alone rather than teaching the separate incomplete-acquisition item immediately beforehand.

title: Distinguish chronic operative risk from current unsuitability
fairness: Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy is the best offered plan for the represented acute gallbladder process with preserved pre-illness function and no new organ instability. Neither age and remote infarction nor antibiotic improvement independently establishes a reason for drainage or interval surgery.

The case requires weighing chronic risk against current fitness and applying that assessment to definitive-treatment timing despite improvement on antibiotics. These are consequential competing considerations, not two successive diagnosis labels.

The actual severity of chronic kidney disease and full anesthetic assessment are not supplied; the item supports a best plan among these choices, not a declaration of universal operative eligibility. No confident clinical error is identified. The options are parallel treatment plans.
This first part is coherent. Its feedback explains the timing/source-control decision but does not disclose the later postoperative antibiotic answer.

title: Reassess postoperative antibiotics after source control
fairness: Stopping routine postoperative biliary antibiotics is the best offered plan after the represented complete source control, absence of complicated or residual infection, and improving clinical course.

The resident must interpret the operative findings as adequate source control and then weigh a still-abnormal but falling white-cell count against the postoperative trajectory. Continuing oral therapy is a credible common error; ongoing intravenous treatment is less compelling but answers the same decision.

The negative operative and infection findings are necessary to establish the antibiotic boundary. They are not a reason to omit clinically important facts to increase difficulty. Stop versus continue is the decision itself, so the key's different verb is not a gratuitous style cue.

The progression from the first part's operation decision to a completed operation is coherent. The current update independently supplies the operation, source-control findings and postoperative course, so it remains answerable without the preceding question. Earlier feedback does not rehearse the antibiotic rule. Difficulty is at the lower end of moderate.

title: Limit an unstable ERCP to effective drainage
fairness: Drainage stenting with staged clearance is the best offered plan when physiology is worsening and a large stone above a tight distal segment requires additional manipulation for extraction.

The two decisions are to limit intervention because of the physiological trajectory and still establish drainage across the persistent obstruction. Sphincterotomy and ending the session is an anatomically relevant near-miss: it can be shorter than extraction yet need not resolve the upstream obstruction.

The supplied guidewire access makes the stenting strategy plausible. Increasing support requirements are necessary clinical observations, not an avoidable cue. All choices are endoscopic plans at the same checkpoint, and the staged key is not uniquely long or qualified. The standalone chronology is clear.

title: Let distal duct anatomy change difficult-stone treatment
fairness: Cholangioscopy-guided fragmentation is the best offered stone-directed strategy after failed standard extraction with a fixed distal duct stricture. Treating proximal duct caliber as permission to dilate the narrowed distal segment is the consequential competing error.

The resident must interpret the caliber/stricture relationship and choose a clearance technique that addresses the stone without applying the inappropriate dilation strategy. Repeat conventional sweeps are a weaker foil, but the large-balloon competitor is clinically relevant.

The pre-existing drainage stent and separate stricture evaluation establish why urgent decompression or a new stricture workup is not the current task. They do not uniquely name the key. No unsupported balloon diameter or universal technical-success claim is made.

This is relevant difficult-duct-stone teaching for surgery residents, although more specialized than initial duct-risk assessment. Actual cholangioscope access and final technique depend on procedural findings; no confident inaccuracy is identified in this best-strategy formulation. The standalone task is clear.

title: Select a bailout when the hilar junction remains unresolved
fairness: Subtotal cholecystectomy is the best offered completion plan for the represented fusion, traction distortion and inability to expose the lower attachment. Neither a fundus-first approach nor conversion by itself establishes safe identification for a committed total operation.

The resident must interpret the apparent funnel as potentially misleading anatomy and then choose an extent of surgery that avoids the unresolved junction. The two total-operation strategies are real operative alternatives, not unrelated foils.

Subtotal is the only limited operation, but that distinction is the actual clinical decision, not a stylistic outlier. There is no pre-answer instruction to preserve tissue or perform a bailout. The explanation appropriately allows conversion and fundus-first reassessment when they genuinely improve safety.
The clinic frame clearly concerns an earlier operative checkpoint. The item stands alone and does not require a missing earlier answer.

title: Map a possible stone-bearing remnant before intervention
fairness: MRCP is the best offered next investigation to characterize the postoperative pouch and its relationship to the ducts, including the incompletely visualized distal duct. There is no demonstrated duct target or represented infection that makes therapeutic ERCP the clearly preferred immediate action.

The resident must combine the prior subtotal operation with a fluid structure containing shadowing foci, then separate anatomical planning from immediate duct intervention or gallbladder functional testing.

The missing duct-connection map is decision-critical anatomical uncertainty; it does not literally repeat the MRCP label. Normal bilirubin between attacks does not negate episodic obstruction. Options are parallel investigations, and the explanation stops short of claiming ultrasound has proved the entire cause of the pain.
The standalone history and task are coherent. This is useful tested postoperative biliary anatomy, though less common than the core acute-cholecystitis and duct-stone decisions.

title: Interpret proximal obstruction beside an impacted neck stone
fairness: MRCP is the best offered initial mapping study for this stable jaundiced patient with a neck stone and disproportionate proximal dilation. ERCP can also define anatomy and provide therapy, but the supplied setting does not establish an urgent drainage need or a routine distal extraction target.

The two consequential judgments are localization from the proximal/distal pattern and selection of anatomical mapping before a potentially misleading routine duct-stone intervention. The syndrome name is not supplied.

The explanation properly treats external compression as a supported possibility rather than proving a fistula subtype or excluding another stricture. No confident clinical inaccuracy is identified; this does not claim ERCP is never appropriate for this syndrome.
The longer HIDA label clarifies its actual target rather than supplying the key. The standalone clinical stage is clear, and this is a high-yield Mirizzi-pattern/safe-operative-planning concept.

title: Drain an infected duct while deferring a high-risk sphincterotomy
fairness: Stenting with staged sphincterotomy/extraction is the single best offered plan for ongoing obstructive infection, excessive anticoagulation and established access across the obstruction.

The resident must balance urgent drainage against the bleeding implications of sphincterotomy, rather than treating drainage and definitive extraction as inseparable. The mechanical-valve history makes anticoagulation management consequential without requiring an invented reversal or bridging regimen.

The phrase 'before any endoscopic drainage' defines the actual delaying strategy being compared. It is broad, but not an unrelated rhetorical absolute: choosing it requires misunderstanding which part of ERCP creates the relevant bleeding risk.

Both immediate extraction and delaying decompression are credible errors. The explanation allows concurrent anticoagulation management and does not prescribe an unsupported time interval. The standalone procedural checkpoint is clear.

title: Interpret an unfinished gallbladder-filling acquisition
clarityIssues: 'Temperature and blood pressure were unchanged' does not establish a stable physiological baseline: the presentation gives fever but no prior blood pressure. The explanation's 'stable checkpoint' is more definite than the visible observations.

cues.phrase: No later images had yet been acquired.
cues.why: A named missing step directly points to 'Continue delayed gallbladder-filling imaging'. Combined with an otherwise normally progressing acquisition, it makes continuation attractive without knowing the diagnostic persistence requirement.

Repeating the stage just performed has no represented acquisition defect or new target. The reader can discard it as redundant, leaving ordinary completion versus acting on an explicitly unfinished study.

fairness: Continuing delayed imaging is the defensible best offered diagnostic plan at a first-hour nonvisualization checkpoint; the explanation appropriately acknowledges morphine augmentation as another accepted route outside the option set.

The high-yield concept is sound, but the item primarily tests one protocol-completion rule. The bowel transit and absent gallbladder do not create a second consequential judgment when the alternatives are surgery from the current acquisition or an unsupported restart.
The absence of earlier/later images is legitimate acquisition information and must not simply be hidden to manufacture difficulty. Its current wording and option set nevertheless give the key away.
This is now a standalone case: no preceding filling-protocol answer is required or visible. The remaining concern is intrinsic cueing and difficulty, not multipart leakage.
suggestions: Replace 'unchanged' with an actual hemodynamic observation or explicitly documented stable blood pressure; do not invent a diagnostic cutoff.

Replace the unsupported restart foil with a clinically plausible plan distinguished by a supported acquisition or patient-specific condition. Re-solve the whole set; do not add morphine augmentation as a supposedly wrong option when it is also appropriate.

If the intended objective remains only first-hour nonvisualization versus completed testing, seek explicit acceptance as an easy foundational item rather than label it a moderate two-step question. Preserve the actual acquisition stage and needed safety information.

title: Reassess early surgery despite several days of symptoms
fairness: Operating during the current admission is the best offered schedule for the supplied symptom/admission chronology and recovered physiology. A rigid early-symptom deadline or initial renal abnormality would lead to inappropriate automatic deferral.

The resident must distinguish the symptom and admission clocks, then decide whether the current physiological course still supports early surgery. The three choices compare schedules for the same operation, and the later dates are clearly constructed alternatives rather than diagnostic thresholds.

The hospital's usual biliary service is relevant feasibility context and does not say which schedule it permits. The physiological observations are concrete rather than an authored fitness conclusion.

The stated WSES timing window is consistent with recalled guidance, but its exact numbers were not freshly source-verified in this no-network review. They should retain their source mapping and clinical review. The task and standalone chronology are intelligible.

title: Choose gallbladder source control during active cardiac deterioration
fairness: Immediate percutaneous gallbladder drainage is the best offered plan alongside cardiac treatment and resuscitation. Persistent gallbladder inflammation plus deterioration makes antibiotic reassessment inadequate as the preferred source-control strategy, while new ischemic findings materially change immediate operative suitability.

The resident must interpret the cardiac trajectory and integrate it with a separately persistent gallbladder source. Neither simply noticing gallstones nor recognizing myocardial injury fully answers the management question.

Both intervention options say 'Immediate', so urgency wording does not uniquely identify the key. Continued antibiotics with reassessment is a real competing plan without an 'alone' caricature. All options address the same immediate gallbladder decision.

The falling blood pressure need not be assigned exclusively to cardiac or infectious shock to rank these offered plans. No specific infarction subtype, drug regimen or post-infarction waiting interval is asserted. The standalone checkpoint is coherent.

title: Choose clearance versus a drainage bridge at a stabilized ERCP
clarityIssues: The task asks for 'the remainder of ... initial ERCP', but one option is percutaneous drainage. It is unclear whether the learner may stop ERCP and change route or must choose the treatment within ERCP.

cues.why: This task wording lets a reader eliminate 'Percutaneous drainage and staged stone extraction' by procedure category without interpreting the physiology or cholangiogram.

fairness: Sphincterotomy and balloon extraction is the defensible best offered plan after stabilization, with normal represented coagulation, established access and an apparently straightforward mobile stone. Stenting with later extraction remains a credible but less favored bridge in this supplied context.

There are two meaningful assessments: current tolerance of intervention and anatomical/technical suitability for clearance. The explicit stone and duct measurements are observations, and the explanation correctly avoids treating them as a universal cutoff.

The third option adds little discrimination because the task prespecifies ERCP and access is already established. This is an option-stage/clarity defect, not a confident clinical error in the intended key.
The item stands alone and contains its necessary admission and procedural findings. The clinical reasoning can remain moderate after repairing the distractor set.
suggestions: Use a neutral complete task such as which immediate biliary treatment plan is best at this procedural checkpoint if changing route is intended to remain possible.

Reassess the percutaneous option even after changing the task: give three credible plans at the same decision stage, each representing a real error distinguished by the supplied physiology or anatomy. Do not make an equally acceptable extraction technique a falsely incorrect third choice.
Preserve the current physiological, coagulation and anatomical observations; do not increase difficulty by removing the facts that make same-session treatment appropriate.

title: Distinguish failed extraction from failed endoscopic drainage access
fairness: A transpapillary plastic stent is the best offered drainage route when extraction has failed but a wire crosses the obstruction, contrast remains upstream, and the patient is deteriorating.

The resident must distinguish retained obstruction from achieved access, then decide whether to use that access for a bridge or abandon it for percutaneous or operative drainage. Failed extraction does not establish failure of the endoscopic route.

Wire position is a legitimate procedural discriminator, not a statement that stent deployment is guaranteed. Actual inability to pass or deploy a drainage device would change the route decision; the explanation does not promise universal technical success.

All three options are actual drainage routes with comparable specificity. The task does not restrict the answer to endoscopy. The standalone sequence is clear, and planned definitive clearance and device removal/exchange are appropriately kept in feedback.

title: Recognize the missing cystic-plate exposure before division
clarityIssues: The request for a 'next dissection step' is narrower than the option 'Clip and divide the two apparent entering structures', which is the division the task already says identification must precede.

cues.phrase: Which next dissection step best completes identification before division
cues.why: The task itself excludes the clip-and-divide option before a learner evaluates the operative findings. It supplies the intended sequencing judgment.

cues.phrase: Gallbladder mobilization is recorded only around the infundibulum
cues.why: After the other two critical-view components are listed, this explicitly partial mobilization points directly to the only gallbladder-mobilization option. The item becomes completion of a familiar checklist rather than two consequential inferences.

fairness: Separating the lower third from the liver bed is the intended and defensible best offered next step if a safe plane is obtainable. Tracing the apparent cystic duct to the common duct is not required to obtain the critical view, and two apparent structures do not by themselves establish it.
The explanation appropriately includes the safe-plane/bailout condition. No confident clinical inaccuracy is identified, and the anatomical concept is very high yield.

The difficulty problem is not cured by calling interpretation of two completed criteria plus one missing criterion two-step reasoning. The task already tells the learner to finish identification rather than divide, leaving one substantive checklist distinction.
The item is standalone; no prior answer leakage is needed for this cue to work.
suggestions: Ask neutrally for the next operative action, so the learner must decide whether identification is sufficient before considering division.

If moderate/hard application is required, add a supported operative observation that makes completion of exposure versus a credible reassessment/bailout strategy consequential, and rebuild parallel alternatives. Do not invent an unsafe plane or force continued dissection to preserve the current key.
Otherwise obtain explicit acceptance of this useful critical-view check as an easy foundational item. Preserve the necessary anatomy rather than hide the missing criterion through vague prose.

title: Treat recurrent obstruction despite an unchanged stent position
fairness: ERCP with stent reassessment/exchange is the best offered immediate drainage plan for recurrent infection and increasing upstream dilation despite unchanged device position, with current upstream wire access achieved.

The resident must distinguish device position from drainage function and distinguish failure of the old device from failure of the current endoscopic route. Percutaneous rescue is a credible alternative if present access or deployment fails; operative exploration is a greater escalation in this represented checkpoint.

Repeating 'stent' in the history and exchange option is necessary identification of the device being managed. It is not sufficient to answer without understanding the evidence of functional obstruction and the available route. The task does not grammatically require an endoscopic answer.

Occlusion is inferred rather than proved by CT. The explanation appropriately leaves the exact maneuver dependent on procedural findings and preserves later stone clearance and device follow-up. The standalone chronology is coherent, with no earlier bridge-stenting answer supplied.
